questions.q: Why does GPU node autoscaling take much longer than typical CPU node autoscaling?
options: GPU nodes are not supported by any cloud autoscaler

Provisioning an H100 node involves attaching high-speed fabric, loading GPU drivers and the NCCL stack, and running health checks before it's usable — minutes to tens of minutes versus under a minute for CPU
GPU nodes autoscale instantly, faster than CPU nodes
Autoscaling only works for stateless web services, never for compute nodes
questions.explain: GPU nodes require substantially more setup (drivers, fabric attachment, NCCL stack, health checks) before they're usable, making scale-up inherently slower than a typical CPU node.

questions.q: In the Karpenter NodePool example, what does limits: nvidia.com/gpu: "512" control?
options: The number of GPUs each individual Pod may request
A hard cap on the total GPUs Karpenter is allowed to provision across the entire NodePool, matching solara-train's hardware ceiling
The minimum number of GPUs required before any node is created
The GPU driver version to install
questions.explain: The limits field on a NodePool caps the aggregate resources Karpenter will provision for that pool, preventing it from provisioning more GPU capacity than actually exists in the account/cluster.

questions.q: How does gang scheduling (Volcano) interact with Karpenter's autoscaling when a job needs more nodes than currently exist?
options: Volcano schedules the job on whatever partial capacity exists, ignoring the shortfall

The job's Pods stay Pending because Volcano won't place a partial gang; those Pending Pods are the signal Karpenter uses to provision the missing nodes, and Volcano only releases the Pods once the full count is Ready
Karpenter and Volcano cannot be used together under any circumstance
Autoscaling disables gang scheduling automatically whenever capacity is short
questions.explain: The two systems compose without special integration: Volcano's gang-scheduling rule keeps Pods Pending until full capacity exists, and those Pending Pods are exactly what triggers Karpenter to provision more nodes.

questions.q: What is the main risk Solara AI guards against when scaling down GPU nodes, and how does it guard against it?
options: The risk of running out of IP addresses; guarded against with a larger subnet
The risk of consolidating away a node that is mid-collective in an active training job; guarded against with a PodDisruptionBudget covering the full replica count
The risk of overpaying for idle CPU nodes; guarded against by disabling autoscaling entirely
The risk of GPU driver version mismatches; guarded against by pinning a single driver version
questions.explain: Scaling down a node actively running training Pods would kill the job mid-collective. Solara AI sets a PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable equal to the full replica count so active training nodes are never eviction/consolidation candidates.

questions.q: What does consolidationPolicy: WhenEmpty with consolidateAfter: 10m accomplish in the NodePool spec?
options: It forces every node to be recreated every 10 minutes regardless of usage
It only removes a node once it has sat completely idle for 10 minutes, avoiding scale-down thrashing for short gaps between jobs
It prevents Karpenter from ever scaling down GPU nodes
It sets the maximum lifetime of any node to 10 minutes
questions.explain: This policy delays removal of an empty node by 10 minutes, which avoids rapidly tearing down and re-provisioning expensive GPU nodes for brief idle periods between jobs.
